A triplet means a group of exactly three things that are closely linked together — usually of the same kind, treated as a single unit, or occurring together.

Think of it this way: just as a "pair" means two things that belong together, a "triplet" means three things that belong together.

1. People — The Most Common Everyday Use

When a mother gives birth to three babies at the same time, those three babies are called triplets. Each individual baby is "a triplet," and together they are "triplets."

"She gave birth to triplets — two boys and a girl."

This is probably the most familiar use of the word. It signals not just that there are three of them, but that they were born together from the same pregnancy. (For comparison: two babies born together are called twins; four are called quadruplets.)

2. Music

In music, a triplet is a group of three notes that are played in the time normally occupied by two notes of the same type.

Here's the simple version: imagine a beat that is usually divided into two equal parts. A triplet squeezes three notes into that same space. This creates a distinctive lilting, rolling, or galloping feel in the music — the rhythm suddenly feels slightly "off" in a pleasing way, because three is being crammed where two would usually go.

You hear triplets a lot in jazz, classical music, and ballads. When a song has that swinging, flowing quality, triplets are often the reason.

"The pianist played a run of triplets in the bridge, giving the passage a smoother, more liquid feel."

The key idea: it's not just three notes — it's three notes deliberately grouped together and fitted into a specific time slot meant for two.

3. Poetry

In poetry, a triplet is a group of three consecutive lines that share a rhyme or are otherwise closely connected as a unit.

"The poem opened with a beautiful triplet, all three lines ending with the same sound."

Sometimes a triplet is called a tercet (another word for the same thing). A famous example is the terza rima, the structure used by the Italian poet Dante, where triplets are linked across stanzas by their rhyme scheme.

The defining feature: the three lines function as a single poetic unit, not just three random lines that happen to follow each other.

4. Mathematics

In mathematics, a triplet (sometimes called an ordered triple) is a set of three numbers or values listed in a specific order, where the order matters.

A common example is coordinates in three-dimensional space. When you describe a point in 3D space, you write three numbers: (x, y, z) — that's a triplet. Swapping the numbers around gives you a different point entirely, which is why the order matters.

"The position of the particle was given by the triplet (3, −1, 7)."

More generally, any time you have three items grouped together as a single structured unit in mathematics, that's a triplet.

5. Genetics and Biology

In genetics, a triplet (also called a codon) is a sequence of three chemical "letters" in DNA or RNA that together code for a specific amino acid — the building blocks of proteins.

Your genetic code is essentially a long string of these triplets, read three letters at a time. Each triplet is a tiny instruction that tells the cell which amino acid to add next when building a protein.

"Each triplet in the DNA sequence corresponds to one amino acid in the protein chain."

The idea is the same as elsewhere: three things grouped and functioning as one unit.

6. General Use

Outside of these specific fields, "triplet" is simply used to describe any group of three matching or related things treated as a unit.

"The designer arranged the photos in a triplet along the wall."
"He scored a triplet of goals in the final ten minutes." (three goals)
"The company launched a triplet of new products on the same day."

Wherever you see three things that go together, function together, or were created/released together, calling them a "triplet" is natural and correct.
What Makes a "Triplet" Different from Just "Three Things"

This is a subtle but important point. Three random apples on a table are not a "triplet." A triplet implies:

  • The three things are of the same kind (three babies, three notes, three lines),
  • They are grouped or linked in some meaningful way (born together, played together, written together),
  • They are often treated as one unit rather than three separate things.

It's the bond between the three that makes them a triplet, not just the number.

SettingWhat a "triplet" means
  • Everyday life: Three babies born at the same time from the same mother.
  • Music: Three notes squeezed into the time normally given to two.
  • Poetry: Three lines grouped together as a unit, often rhyming.
  • Mathematics: An ordered set of three values treated as one unit.
  • Genetics: A sequence of three DNA/RNA letters that code for one amino acid.
  • General: Any group of three closely related, same-kind things treated as a unit.

The thread running through every single use is the same: three things, bonded together, functioning as one.
